result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.preferential_attachment()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute preferential attachment score for node pairs. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L16612-L16706){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.preferential_attachment(ebunch=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Preferential attachment](/assets/graphs/preferential-attachment.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Nodes B and E are outlined in the accent color and every edge touching them is in accent; badges give B degree 3 and E degree 4. Shared neighbors play no role: the card multiplies the two degrees, 3 times 4, for a score of 12." width="100%"} For each pair of nodes `(u, v)`, computes `|N(u)| × |N(v)|`, the product of their degrees. Based on the "rich get richer" principle where high-degree nodes are more likely to acquire new connections. Unlike the other link-prediction scores, it ignores shared neighbors entirely: two hubs in different parts of the graph can score highly even if they have nothing in common. The graph is not modified. This is useful for: - link prediction in growing networks where new edges attach to popular nodes (citation networks, the web, many online platforms) - a degree-only baseline against which neighborhood-based scores such as `common_neighbors()` or `adamic_adar_index()` can be judged - quickly scoring pairs whose neighborhoods don't overlap at all (where neighborhood scores are all zero) Degrees here count distinct neighbors, so parallel edges are not double counted and an isolated node always produces a score of `0`. On a directed graph, the *out-degree* of each node is used. When `ebunch=` is `None`, every pair of non-adjacent nodes is scored, which is quadratic in the number of nodes; pass `ebunch=` on large graphs. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ebunch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[Union[int, str], Union[int, str]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of `(u, v)` node pairs to score. Each node can be given as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). Pairs are scored even if `u` and `v` are already connected, and they are returned in the order given. If `None` (the default), all pairs of nodes that are not already connected (in either direction) are scored, each unordered pair once, in no particular order. A node that doesn't exist raises a `ValueError`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[tuple[int, int, int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of `(u, v, score)` tuples where `score` is `degree(u) × degree(v)`. Nodes are reported as node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If a node in `ebunch=` does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Preferential attachment scores a pair by the product of their degrees: $\mathrm{PA}(u, v) = |N(u)| \cdot |N(v)|$. It uses no local structure at all, just two degree lookups, and it embodies the Barabási-Albert "rich get richer" dynamic that produces scale-free networks. As a link predictor it works well where degree distributions are heavy-tailed but tends to overrank hub-hub pairs that share nothing else in common. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a star with hub `1` and leaves `2` to `5`, two leaves each have degree 1, so their score is `1`. Node `6` is isolated (degree 0), so any pair involving it scores `0`: ::: {#0f9be534 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_star_graph(5) # hub node 1 with degree 4 graph.add_node() # node 6, isolated graph.preferential_attachment([(2, 3), (2, 6)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [(2, 3, 1), (2, 6, 0)] ``` ::: ::: Because it ignores neighborhood overlap, preferential attachment can rank a pair highly even when they share no neighbors. Below are two separate stars with hubs `1` and `5` (degree 3 each). The hubs score `9` despite having zero common neighbors, while two leaves of the same star share their hub but score only `1`: ::: {#959c67ab .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_star_graph(4) # hub 1, leaves 2-4 graph.add_star_graph(4) # hub 5, leaves 6-8 pairs = [(1, 5), (2, 3)] list(zip(graph.preferential_attachment(pairs), graph.common_neighbors(pairs))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [((1, 5, 9), (1, 5, 0)), ((2, 3, 1), (2, 3, 1))] ``` ::: :::
